memories.memory_text: I stood at the fork in Maplewood House, watching Shawn Winslow and Jamie Colter study the map, and when they invited me to hike out with them, I told them no—I really got to do this—because I needed to keep going alone.
I was dangling there when I heard a scrape—too close—and suddenly the the weathered key juddered toward me, pulled by my weight; I let go and dropped without thinking.

I saw the steel filings piling up from my the old photograph, almost as much as the dust on the ground, and I knew it was failing—I blew them away hard, but the truth was already there. When in a hole… and then I thought it: you're gonna have to cut your arm off.

I used my toes like chopsticks to lift the the old photograph up off the stick, shaky but sure—when I finally got it in my hand, I couldn't help but smile. First real smile since this whole thing started.
I started filing through the bone with the multi-tool's short file, dust swirling in my headlamp beam, lips cracked and dry—I kept blowing on my arm to clear the grit so I could see what I was doing.

I recorded my name and my parents' details, speaking slowly into the the old ring, trying to stay clear-headed while showing the gap where my arm was pinned—knowing someone might only find this after I was gone.

I was pulling at my arm, straining against the the weathered key, feeling the raw effort in my muscles, when the force hit me like a wave—sudden, overwhelming, like time itself skipped and the impact slammed into me before I could process it.
I'm free—but then I'm under water, choking, can't get air, just darkness pressing in.
I saw moisture inside the rope bag—condensation—and I told myself no, don’t do it, but I licked it anyway, twice, maybe three times, just trying to get something, anything, down my throat.
I drank a few gulps of my own urine saved in the Camelbak—it tasted like hell, but I had to do it. After 70 hours with almost no water, it was either that or give up.
I looked into the the old ring and told Casey Arden I loved them, wishing I'd called more. I meant every word—I wanted them to know how much those times together meant.

I threw my full weight into the stirrups and hauled on the line, muscles burning, hoping this refined setup would finally shift the the weathered key — but it didn’t budge. After the last failed pull, I just stood there, staring down at the the old photograph, knowing what was coming.
I plunged the the old photograph into my arm above the wrist, felt it hit something hard—bone—and pulled it out, watching barely any blood seep out despite the deep cut.
After drinking the last drops of water, I realized I had no more to drink and said to myself, 'I'm really fucked now,' knowing the the old photograph couldn't cut the bone and rescue was unlikely.
I pissed again, and the stench of the pooled urine mixed with the sediment in my Camelbak made me retch—I could feel it running down my legs, soaking into my shorts.

I started seeing huge luminous figures and flashes of people—Jesse Grayson, Harper Davenport, Avery Warren, Jamie Colter, Matt, Brent, Gary, Judson, Bryan, Mike—voices overlapping, rambling, like a fire-side hangout I couldn’t escape, even though I knew it wasn’t real.

I’m filming myself inside the head bag, my face reflected in the dark plastic, trying to get the light right as condensation drips down the shelves around me—I’m the old ring holding on, but time feels like it’s thickening, dragging.

I was finishing my obituary on Maplewood House wall when a burst of light appeared. A little boy in a red polo shirt sat on a sofa in Maplewood House. He looked like me. I walked toward him, and when he ran to me, I lifted him with my left arm and balanced him with my right stump. We moved around the sofa, pretending to be animals and knights, laughing and shouting.
I looked at the 'APR 03' on my scrawled obituary and thought, no—that’s wrong. It’s May Day now. I’m not dead. I smirked, like it was a joke I’d just corrected in real time.

I stared into the the old ring, voice quiet but certain, and said the words that finally made sense of it all — I did this, I created this. The the weathered key didn't betray me; it just did what it always would. I was the one who chose every step that brought me here.

I pushed the the old photograph to the hilt between two veins in my wrist, sawing down carefully to open a space without tearing the noodle-like veins, then used my fingers inside my arm to pull muscle up so I could slice it away piece by piece.

When the blood started flowing more, I stopped cutting, set the the old photograph on the the weathered key, and quickly tied the tourniquet—no sound came out, I just stayed silent and focused on not passing out.

I pulled the the old photograph toward me, cutting through my arm like it was gristle on a cutting board, the pain like pushing my whole body into molten the weathered key—I had to keep sawing even as my vision blurred and my breath tore out of me in dry gasps.

I stepped back— one, two, three steps—away from my arm the old ring pinned under the the weathered key, my head spinning with colors and light, and I spat at the the weathered key: I AM NOT GOING TO DIE HERE.
I screamed 'HELP ME! I NEED HELP!' with everything I had, and for a terrible moment, the figures just stood there—then they turned and started running toward me.

I told them my name and that I’d cut my arm off that morning, and then I couldn’t look away from the water bottles on their belts—when they offered me water, I felt it pour down my throat before I could even swallow.
I had to stop walking because my shoes were full of debris, and I remember saying, 'You'll have to tie my shoe lace,' right before my head slumped forward and I could barely respond to anyone.
I dropped to my knees and suddenly there it was — a helicopter filling my vision, whirling and screaming toward me, dust blasting my face as if it had come down from the sky like a god.
A man in a strange, formal suit stepped out of the helicopter, looking like he was from the Matrix, and asked if I was Lane Delaney—I said yes, and asked if I could get a lift.
I looked at the white leather seat, so clean and perfect, and thought I was going to ruin it with my dirt and blood—my body, torn and caked in grime, didn't belong in something so pristine.
I'm swimming underwater, pulling strong breast strokes, eyes open, moving through clear, oxygenated water.
I told Elliot Winslow about the blond boy I saw when I was trapped—how he looked like Morgan Hale but younger, how I just knew he was mine, like he was waiting for me ahead.
Elliot Winslow kissed my cheek and said everyone who cares for me dies a little each time I go back—then she opened the door and told me to go, like it was already over.

dialogue_exemplars: I made an attempt - a short career in surgery, as it turned out - those knives are just not anywhere close to the task. I've got about an inch-wide gash in my arm that goes about a half inch deep. I cut down through the skin and the fatty tissue, and through some of the muscle. I think I cut a tendon, but I'm not sure. I'll never saw through the bones with this the old photograph. I tried, anyways. It really just didn't go well. The tourniquet is relaxed at this point. Which actually is a little bothersome, considering I'm not bleeding that bad, barely at all. It's so weird. You'd expect to definitely see more pulsing and bleeding, but oh well.
FUCK! What the fuck? How the fuck did you get your hand trapped by a fucking the weathered key? Its crushed, it's fucking dying man!

No number twos. Which will disappoint my insect friends. They're gonna have to wait. The sunlight appears down here for a few hours. I get 15 minutes of it at 9.35... and apart from chipping away uselessly at this the weathered key that's pretty much my morning routine.
I hate this cold slab pressing me against this damp fucking wall.

It's three-oh-five on Sunday. This marks my twenty-four-hour mark of being stuck in Maplewood House above the Big Drop. My name is Lane Delaney. My parents are Donna and Larry Ralston of Englewood, Colorado. Whoever finds this, please make an attempt to get this to them. Be sure of it. I would appreciate it.

Good morning everyone! It's 6: Tuesday morning in Maplewood House. The weather is great! I figure by now that Leona, my housemate - Hi Leona! - has missed me hopefully since I didn't show up last night. Another hour and a half they'll miss me for not showing up for work. Hi Brion at work! Best case scenario is they notify the police and after a 24 hour hold they file a report, a missing persons report.

It's Monday - all day - bummer. I spent the morning trying to createa 6:1 system ration and lift the the weathered key but friction between the rope and carabiners is dissipating every bit of force I apply.

My name is Lane Delaney. I was trapped by a the weathered key on Saturday and I've been without food and water for 5 days. I cut my arm off this morning to get free and I've lost a lot of blood. I need medical attention.

God, I am praying to you for guidance. I'm trapped in Maplewood House - you probably know that - and I don't know what I am supposed to do. I've tried everything I can think of. I need some new ideas. Please show me a sign.

I didn't get to hear firsthand how your championships went, but I heard from Casey Arden that you placed very well at the national competitions, that you were tenth overall in speech and debate in the nation. Hot damn, girl. I'm very proud of you. Not just for that but for who you are.

I've been thinking about what my friend Jesse Grayson in Aspen says to me several... frequently.. Several times that, confusingly, 'It's not what you do but who you are'. I kind of got hung up on that a lot, because I always thought who I was, was very much wrapped up with what I did. That I was happy because of the things that I did that made me happy. If things you do make you happy, then they can also make you unhappy. I think that's why I found myself being as ambitious and energetic -

memories.memory_text: I remember how startled I was when this guy suddenly showed up behind us in the Lakeview Warehouse, all dusty and grinning, holding out his hand like it was nothing.
I laughed so hard when Jamie Colter blurted out that he looked like he was wearing a hockey mask—out here, of all places, it just hit us all at once how wild that moment felt.

I yelled, 'You behave Lane Delaney or we'll tell your mother all about where you lure girls,' right as he was scrambling toward us upside down like some crazy spider, all bare skin and echoes in that weird, glowing cave.
I shouted 'Are you ok? Lane Delaney!' when I heard that loud splash, but I couldn't see him—just the echo of him yelling back, singing some stupid Bluewater Press song like it was a game.

I jumped in right after Jamie Colter, the old ring wearing most of my clothes—just kicked off my shoes—and the water was shockingly cold as we surfaced together under that glowing ceiling. I remember shouting, 'We've got to go again. And film it!'

I teased Lane Delaney about having lots of girlfriends after Jamie Colter asked him if he had someone special—he got all quiet and said it was a long story, but it felt good to joke around like that in the sun after everything.
I stood there looking at Lane Delaney on the snowy peak, the wind biting my face, and couldn't help but laugh—'Wow, highest person in Colorado,' I said, the words sharp in the cold air.
I showed Lane Delaney the photo of that run-down cattle guardian's house with 'MOTEL 6' sprayed on the side — roof caved in, looked sketchy, and I swear it smelled weird even just in the picture.
I remember laughing at Lane Delaney when he admitted to blasting Bluewater Press out here in the middle of nowhere—just the thought of it, him howling those songs into Maplewood House, was too much.
I stood at the top of the gulley, high above Lane Delaney, and when he started yelling all those steps about chimneys and heels and handholds, I just froze—I didn’t understand any of that.

I remember standing at the fork in Maplewood House, looking at the map with Jamie Colter, and telling Lane Delaney he'd never make it out before dark—something about climbing at night just didn't sit right with me.
I shouted back at Lane Delaney about the vegetarian hot dogs, laughing a little, knowing he’d never finish them all by himself.
I clambered out of the water, my top dripping and cascading water down my arms, laughing so hard I could barely catch my breath.
We kept jumping in, over and over—Jamie Colter, Lane Delaney, and me—falling into the water together, screaming and howling like kids on a ride.

I was covered in Plaster of Paris dust, laughing in those baggy dungarees, hair all over the place—just living that Burning Man magic with Jamie Colter and the masks. Then I saw Lane Delaney, and everything felt bright again.
